movie.title: The Dog Stars
movie.overview: After the world's population has been ravaged by a pandemic, a man lives a lonesome existence in a Colorado airplane hangar with his dog and a dour gunman he has befriended. When a mysterious transmission comes through on the radio while he’s flying his old Cessna, it sparks a hunt for the provenance of the sound.

reviews.author: Brent Marchant
reviews.content: Life in a post-apocalyptic world is a common theme in movies (especially, if you believe what’s published in the media, the increasing prospect that such an outcome may be coming closer to a reality than any of us might like). In many cases, these films follow the experiences of a resourceful, innovative protagonist who quietly but skillfully struggles to survive, successfully managing to fend off foes while cerebrally wrestling with feelings about what’s been lost. That scenario is apparent once again in this latest release from legendary director Ridley Scott. Unfortunately, however, this is not one of the filmmaker’s better efforts, a blatantly uneven production that gets things right in some regards but woefully misses the mark in others. Based on the 2012 novel of the same name by Peter Heller, the film follows the life of a mechanic and antique Cessna pilot, Hig (Jacob Elordi), who ekes out a comparatively comfortable existence in the Colorado wilderness with his wise-cracking marksman wingman, Bangley (Josh Brolin), in a dystopian future that has been devastated by a deadly virus. Like Hig and Bangley, pockets of survivalists resistant to the pandemic’s lethal impact are scattered across the countryside, but they face constant danger from the encroachment of ruthless scavengers seeking to pilfer whatever they can find for themselves. But, despite the undeniable harshness of this new reality, Hig still pines for a way of life that once was. And he’s convinced of rediscovering that possibility when he receives radio messages from a mystery woman (Allison Janney) in Grand Junction, CO that ambiguously hold out hope for the existence of such a sanctuary. In his quest to find the truth, he embarks on an adventure-filled journey in which he encounters a variety of other survivors, such as Aaron (Bendict Wong), head of a surprisingly thriving Mennonite community, and a hard-nosed gun-toting rancher, Jack (a.k.a. “Pops”) (Guy Pearce), living in a remote and vulnerable locale with his daughter, Cima (Margaret Qualley). But can Hig survive the journey? And what might he find if he ever makes it to Grand Junction? While the premise here is solid, recalling such offerings as “I Am Legend” (2007) and films in the “Mad Max” franchise, the finished product nevertheless occasionally teeters on shaky ground. After a strong but sometimes-slow opening hour, backed by a reasonably commendable closing act, in between viewers are mercilessly subjected to a middle segment that *seriously* defies believability, taking the picture decidedly off the rails, a serious blow to the film’s overall credibility. This is truly regrettable, as this disproportionately out-of-place sequence makes it easy for viewers to quickly lose interest as the project struggles to get back on track before the credits roll. It’s difficult to fathom what the filmmaker was going for in such a ridiculously over-the-top sequence, and it detracts from the elements that truly work well (a terrific cast, gorgeous cinematography, and an emotive soundtrack reminiscent of Scott’s earlier cinematic opus, “Thelma & Louise” (1991)). I can’t help but think that this was a case of failure to “kill one’s darlings,” and, in this instance, that shortcoming nearly undermines all of the audience goodwill the picture amasses before and after it. What’s more, the script is short on its back story elements, leaving one wondering how the narrative ultimately arrived at where it is. Sadly, “The Dog Stars” could have been *much* better, both as a cautionary tale and as a fine work of big screen drama, with some deliberate tweaking. As it stands now, though, the survival considerations addressed here could be just as applicable to viewing audiences as they are to the characters themselves.

reviews.author: TheStoic
reviews.content:
What a great movie!! One of those worth seeing in the theater—and one that leaves you hoping for a sequel!

Great story, great actors, great direction!

No racial quotas, no trendy interracial couples, and no gender issues shoved down our throats—in short, no “woke” garbage! A breath of fresh air. I want more of this.

I highly recommend it! I’m looking forward to a sequel!

reviews.author: Manuel São Bento
reviews.content:
Check out my full review @ https://www.manuelsbento.com/the-dog-stars-2026-ridley-scotts-gorgeous-grief-stricken-post-apocalypse-never-quite-takes-flight/

Rating: C+

THE DOG STARS is a gorgeous, contemplative post-apocalyptic thriller that never fully earns its two-hour runtime. Ridley Scott finds real tenderness in a story about grief, isolation, and the fragile work of learning to hope again, and the ensemble cast sells that journey beautifully. But the screenplay leans too hard on familiar genre beats and repetitive detours, leaving even its most striking visuals feeling more decorative than purposeful. A film that looks and sounds wonderful, but rarely says anything new.

aiEnrichment.summary_one_sentence: In a post-apocalyptic Colorado, a lonely pilot and his dog embark on a high-stakes search for hope after picking up a mysterious radio transmission on his vintage airplane.
aiEnrichment.summary_short: Years after a catastrophic pandemic wipes out most of humanity, Hig survives in a secluded Colorado airfield alongside his faithful dog and a cynical, heavily armed neighbor. Life consists of routine patrols and scavenging until a distant, faint signal reaches the radio of Hig's old Cessna. Driven by the possibility of finding other survivors and a better life beyond their isolated sanctuary, Hig risks everything to trace the origin of the mysterious sound.
aiEnrichment.summary_long: In the wake of a devastating global flu pandemic that has decimated the world's population, Hig leads a quiet, solitary life based out of an abandoned Colorado airplane hangar. His only constant companions are his beloved dog, Jasper, and Bangley, a dour, gun-toting survivalist who helps defend their perimeter against hostile scavengers. While Hig spends his days taking to the skies in his 1958 Cessna to scout the surrounding area, he remains deeply haunted by grief and loneliness. One afternoon, during a routine flight that pushes the limits of his fuel supply, his radio picks up a faint, unexpected voice transmission coming from a far-off point. The brief sound shatters Hig's resignation to isolation, igniting a desperate hope that life, community, and safety might exist beyond his immediate horizons. Despite warnings from the pragmatic Bangley about the lethal dangers of the unknown wasteland, Hig decides he cannot ignore the signal. Preparing his plane for a journey beyond his point of no return, he sets off across the ruined American landscape to hunt down the provenance of the sound. Along the way, he must navigate treacherous territories, unforgiving weather, and the lingering threat of hostile survivors. Ultimately, his journey becomes a deeply personal quest not just for physical survival, but for human connection, redemption, and a reason to keep living.
aiEnrichment.synopsis:
Set in a bleak post-apocalyptic world ravaged by a deadly pandemic, *The Dog Stars* follows Hig, a civilian pilot living a fragile, quiet existence in an abandoned Colorado airfield. Bound by routine, Hig survives alongside his devoted dog, Jasper, and Bangley, a gruff, militant neighbor who guards their sanctuary from outside threats. While Bangley focuses entirely on defense and practical survival, Hig longs for the warmth, connection, and humanity lost to the past.

Everything changes when Hig catches a unexpected voice transmission over his Cessna's radio during a flight near the edge of his safe zone. Though vague and fleeting, the signal suggests that a functional community might exist somewhere past the mountains. Torn between the relative safety of his current life and the irresistible promise of hope, Hig makes the daring choice to venture beyond his known territory. The story explores themes of grief, resilience, and the enduring human spirit as one man risks everything to find out if he is truly alone in the world.

story_structure.climax: Hig must confront the immediate physical threats and emotional vulnerabilities of integrating with this new group, overcoming mistrust and external hazards while deciding whether to return to his old life or forge a new path.
story_structure.conflict: Hig is torn between the bleak, controlled safety of his hangar enclave and a deep longing for human connection, hope, and life beyond their isolated perimeter. This tension reaches a turning point when he decides to investigate a faint radio transmission he heard years earlier beyond their usual flight boundary.
story_structure.resolution: Hig bridges his past and future by connecting the canyon survivors with Bangley back at the airfield, ultimately establishing a new, shared existence grounded in companionship, renewal, and hope.
story_structure.introduction: In a post-apocalyptic Colorado, Hig survives at an abandoned airfield with his aging dog, Jasper, and his strictly defensive, gun-toting neighbor, Bangley. Hig spends his days flying his 1956 Cessna 182, clinging to memories of the past and mourning the loss of his wife and the old world.
story_structure.risingAction: Hig undertakes a perilous solo flight past the 'point of no return' into unknown territory, risking running out of fuel or encountering hostile survivors. Upon landing in a secluded canyon, he discovers a small family community living in isolation, including a young woman named Cima and her father.
